advantages: Naming the model makes the project comparable to others in the same revenue class, instead of to every blockchain project.
The four questions expose cost early: the payer and the value-accrual holder are identified before any infrastructure is bought.
The same four questions give a one-line description of any company, which is exactly what a comparison question asks for.
A model can be tested for coherence - if the payer and the value-accrual holder differ, a transfer of money between them has to be designed.
It separates the technology decision from the commercial decision, so a failed project can be diagnosed without blaming the protocol.
limitations: The four questions describe the shape of the arrangement but not the price, the margin or the market size - they are a framework, not a business plan.
They are post-hoc: a project that has already been built usually has to be reverse-fitted into one of the answers, and the fit can be uncomfortable.
The framework does not tell you whether the chain is needed at all - a database is often the right answer and no model in this unit covers that case.
Two firms can describe the same revenue flow in very different ways, so the labels overlap and the taxonomy is a convenience, not a law.
Applied to a token project, the framework can make an unviable design look tidy, because the fourth question answers 'what is tokenised' without asking whether anyone wants the token.
Introduction to Blockchain Business Mode.memoryTrick: **Who runs it, who pays, where value lands, what is tokenised** - the four questions, asked in that order.
Introduction to Blockchain Business Mode.modernNote: The taxonomy in the syllabus was written in the 2017-2019 token boom. Most enterprise chains today are permissioned and tokenless, so the four questions still apply but the fourth answer is usually 'nothing', and the real market has consolidated into a small number of BaaS and platform vendors.

examAnswer.question: Define a blockchain business model and explain it using the four questions every such model must answer.
examAnswer.full:
A blockchain business model is the commercial arrangement behind a blockchain project: it specifies who runs the network, who pays to run it, where the value the network creates accrues, and what exactly gets tokenised on the ledger. The technology decides what is technically possible; the model decides whether the project survives, because it is the model that turns a working ledger into revenue.

**1. Who runs the network.** Either a provider that operates it as a managed service (BaaS or a platform), a consortium whose members jointly run it, or a set of independent node operators. Each carries a different cost base and a different liability for downtime.

**2. Who pays.** Somebody funds the recurring running costs - hosting, security, key custody, upgrades, node operations and governance. The payer is frequently neither the user nor the operator; in a consortium it is the sponsoring members, which is why membership fees are the standard instrument.

**3. Where the value accrues.** The value the network creates ends up in exactly one of five places: the operator's service fee, the marketplace's take-rate, the software vendor's licence, the consultancy's invoice, or the token holder's balance. This is the question that identifies the model, and it is where the four risks (operating, liquidity, adoption, token) attach.

**4. What is tokenised.** Nothing at all, a utility right to use the network, or a claim on an issuer. Tokenisation is a design choice, not a requirement - most enterprise chains are permissioned and tokenless.

**The coherence test.** The answers have to work together. The operator creates the cost, the payer covers it, and the value-accrual holder must be able to cover it too. Where the payer and the value-accrual holder are different parties - the common case in a consortium - an explicit transfer of money between them has to be designed into the model, or the chain is quietly underfunded and its quality decays until members leave.

advantages: Makes the running costs of a shared ledger visible - hosting, security, key custody, upgrades and governance - instead of absorbing them into somebody's IT budget.
Gives the free-rider problem a price: membership or usage fees make non-contribution observable to every member.
Supplies the contribution incentive that makes data sharing rational, which is what makes the shared record worth anything.
Forces governance and exit rules to be written down before the first dispute, when they are cheap to write.
Allows the model to be audited annually against real usage - collected fees versus actual cost - so underfunding is caught while it is still cheap to fix.
limitations: Fees that cover the cost can exceed the value members get, and then the chain is correctly abandoned - pricing is a knife edge.
Usage-based fees punish smaller members and effectively exclude them, which can hollow out the consortium's data coverage.
A shared ledger that few people trust will not collect fees no matter how well the model is designed; adoption precedes revenue.
Governance written down at the start ages badly as the chain, its membership and its regulation change.
The model can be used to justify a fee rise that kills participation, so 'the members should pay more' is not automatically the right answer.
Need for blockchain business models.memoryTrick: **Cost, payer, price for free riders, incentive to share, governance, review** - the ledger dies of all six.
Need for blockchain business models.modernNote: Consortium chains today mostly fund themselves through member subscription and cloud credits from a sponsoring member, with the sponsorship itself being the real business model - which is why consortium survival tracks the sponsor's balance sheet, not the consortium's charter.

examAnswer.question: Why does a shared ledger need an explicit business model? What happens in a consortium when nobody pays for the ledger?
examAnswer.full:
A shared ledger needs an explicit business model because technology alone does not answer who funds it or why anybody contributes to it. A blockchain replaces a trusted institution's records with a network, but it does not remove the network's costs - it relocates them.

**1. Name the running costs.** Hosting and node operation, security audits and patching, key management, protocol upgrades and governance, node onboarding, and the staff who answer incidents. These recur every year for as long as the chain exists.

**2. Assign the payer.** Membership fee per consortium member, fee per transaction, subscription per seat, or a funded treasury. This decides who has a stake in the chain's health and who has a vote when money is short.

**3. Price the free-rider problem.** Every member values the shared record; every member under-contributes to it. Membership or usage fees make non-contribution visible to all, and linking the fee to actual use makes hoarding more expensive than contributing.

**4. Build the contribution incentive.** Priority transaction ordering, lower fees, access to shared data, governance weight, or a share of treasury rewards. If contributing data earns nothing, everyone hoards and the shared record stays empty.

**5. Settle governance and exit.** Who votes on upgrades, how a member leaves and what happens to its data, and what happens if the sponsoring member walks away. Consortiums fail on governance long before they fail on technology.

**6. Review against reality.** Compare collected fees with the running cost every year. Fees below cost mean the chain is subsidised and fragile; fees above the value members get mean members leave.

**What actually happens when nobody pays.** The ledger is quietly underfunded: nodes are not upgraded, security patches are delayed, key custody is handled ad hoc, and the shared record's quality decays. Participants then contribute less because the record is less reliable, which reduces its value further - the classic collapse of a public good without a funding mechanism.

advantages: The five classical models are proven revenue mechanics with known failure modes, so a blockchain project can start from a tested template.
Subscription and licence translate cleanly into managed-service and software-product pricing on a permissioned, tokenless chain.
Marketplace mechanics make the take-rate question unavoidable, which is where most blockchain economics arguments actually happen.
Freemium explains why a chain may subsidise a free tier and who ends up paying for it.
Professional services gives a fast, honest cash-flow bridge while a product is being built.
limitations: Every classical model earned from trust, and the shared ledger commoditises trust - so copying a model onto a chain usually copies the cost and loses the revenue.
Subscription and licence revenue scale linearly with customers and cannot capture value created on the network itself.
Marketplace economics collapse when the ledger removes the very risk the take-rate was paid to insure against.
Freemium is hard to fund on a chain because the free tier consumes real node resources that somebody must pay for.
Professional services income is capped by headcount and creates no lock-in, so it cannot fund a long platform build on its own.
Traditional business models.memoryTrick: **Same models, counterparty swapped for a ledger** - subscription, licence, marketplace, freemium, services; each breaks where the trust used to sit.

examAnswer.question: Compare the traditional business models with blockchain business models. Where does each traditional model break down?
examAnswer.full:
Blockchain business models are not invented from scratch - they are classical models with the counterparty replaced by a shared ledger and the middleman cut out. Take each in turn.

**Subscription** sells continued access over time: the customer pays a recurring fee for the right to keep using the service. On a chain this becomes a managed service in which the recurring fee buys guaranteed node uptime and an SLA. Its blockchain-specific problem is that without a token there is no natural recurring payment instrument, so the chain must be sold contractually.

**Licence** sells a permanent right to a copy: the customer buys the code once. On a chain the customer buys the client software and smart contracts and then runs the nodes, hosts the contracts and pays the gas itself. The break is small here - this model transfers well.

**Marketplace** takes a cut of transactions between strangers: the platform supplies trust and matching. On a chain the ledger supplies the trust record directly, so the take-rate has to shrink or be replaced by a subscription. This is where the largest revenue disruption happens.

**Freemium** gives a basic tier free and charges for premium features. On a chain the free tier still consumes real node resources, so somebody must fund it - usually the premium tier's fees - and the free tier must be capped or it is a pure cost.

**Professional services** sells expertise for a project fee or a retainer: advisory, integration and managed operations. It transfers almost unchanged, and it is the fastest revenue available - but income is capped by headcount.

**The common break.** Every classical model earned from being the trusted party, and the shared ledger commoditises exactly that trust. So the cost falls but the revenue must be rebuilt somewhere else - in a token, in a subscription, or in a service contract. The models do not fail because blockchains are different; they fail because the thing they were paid for has been made cheaper.

advantages: The classification rests on one question - where the money comes from - so any project can be placed in seconds from its revenue flow.
It separates models with genuinely different risk profiles, which is what a comparison answer needs.
It matches the way firms actually earn: a real company usually runs two or three of these at once, and the taxonomy describes the combination.
It links directly to the exam shape: a named company can be identified from a one-line revenue description.
Each model has an obvious failure condition, so the taxonomy doubles as a risk checklist.
limitations: The boundaries blur: a BaaS vendor with a marketplace on top and a services arm fits three classes at once, so the label can mislead.
Revenue source does not reveal the margin, the capital intensity or the customer concentration.
The P2P class contains the widest spread of outcomes, from a well-funded chain to a token with no users.
It says nothing about governance, decentralisation or who controls the rules - two very different projects can share a model.
Real firms deliberately blur it, so the model is a description of the revenue flow rather than a classification of the firm.
Types of Blockchain Business Models.memoryTrick: **Money from: infrastructure, trades, code, expertise, token** - and each one carries its own risk: operating, liquidity, adoption, capacity, price.
Types of Blockchain Business Models.modernNote: The 2019-era expectation that most projects would be P2P token networks did not hold. The live market is dominated by BaaS and platform models for enterprises, marketplace models for exchanges and trading venues, and software products for tooling - the P2P/token class now largely survives as infrastructure providers and a small number of consumer chains.

examAnswer.question: Explain the types of blockchain business model (BaaS, marketplace, platform/infrastructure, software products, professional services and P2P). Compare them and identify which model a named company is running.
examAnswer.full:
Blockchain business models are classified by where the money comes from. This is the classifying question, and it fixes the customer, the risk profile and the way the model scales. Six types.

**1. BaaS (Blockchain as a Service).** The provider runs the ledger as a managed service - nodes, consensus, key custody, monitoring, upgrades - under an SLA, and the customer keeps its business logic and data model. Priced per transaction, per seat or per tier. *Risk:* operating and uptime liability; the provider carries it. *Example:* a bank paying a vendor to run its permissioned chain.

**2. Platform / infrastructure.** The provider sells the protocol, the tooling and the developer platform that other people build on, rather than running a chain for a customer. Revenue grows with the ecosystem it enables rather than with one client's volume. *Example:* a foundation that runs a public chain and sells SDKs, node tooling and hosted services.

**3. Marketplace.** The platform brokers transactions between members and takes a cut, so revenue scales directly with transaction volume. *Risk:* liquidity risk - a thin market gives thin revenue. *Example:* an exchange taking 0.1-2% of trades.

**4. Software products.** The vendor sells a licence or a subscription for code; the customer runs the nodes, hosts the contracts and pays the gas. High margin, near-zero operational load, but no lock-in and no share of the value the customer creates on the chain. *Risk:* adoption risk against open-source equivalents.

**5. Professional services.** Advisory on architecture and governance, integration into the client's systems, and managed operations under a retainer. Paid for effort and expertise, not for network usage. *Risk:* income is capped by the number of billable people. *Example:* a consultancy paid 40% of a bank's integration project.

**6. P2P.** Participants transact directly with each other over the shared ledger and there is no platform transaction to tax. The coordinator is paid by the network - token holdings or issuance, routing, liquidity, oracle and staking services - so its revenue grows with the health of the whole network. *Risk:* if the token never gains value, the revenue disappears.

**The comparison.** Each model has a different risk profile: operating risk for BaaS, ecosystem risk for a platform, liquidity risk for a marketplace, adoption risk for software, capacity risk for services and token risk for P2P. Each also scales differently - software scales with copies, marketplace with volume, platform with the ecosystem, P2P with network value, services with headcount.

**In practice and in the exam.** Most firms run several models at once - a BaaS platform with a marketplace on top and a services arm - so when asked to identify a named company's model, quote the revenue flow first ('it charges a monthly SLA to run a permissioned chain for a bank'), name the dominant model (BaaS), and then note the supporting ones.

advantages: The customer gets the capability without blockchain operations staff, node procurement, key management or incident response - it buys certainty rather than parts.
Predictable pricing: a fixed SLA fee replaces the open-ended cost of running infrastructure and hiring specialists.
Fast time to first transaction - weeks instead of the months a consortium takes to stand up a governance body and a node estate.
The provider carries the operational and security burden, including uptime liability and key custody.
It is the only sensible entry point for tokenless, permissioned enterprise chains, so it is where most commercial blockchain activity actually is.
limitations: The customer gives up control of the infrastructure and, critically, of the keys - the provider is the custody and trust boundary, and that is a real concentration of risk.
The customer is locked to the provider's tooling, governance and upgrade schedule, and migrating a live chain to another provider is hard.
The economics favour the provider: hosting, keys and SLA obligations are the provider's costs and the customer's fees.
A managed chain still has to be justified - many of these workloads would run more cheaply on a conventional database and messaging system.
Regulatory and data-residency requirements can make a multi-tenant managed chain unacceptable, forcing the customer back to self-running.
Blockchain as a Service (BaaS).memoryTrick: **Provider runs: nodes, consensus, keys, monitoring, upgrades, SLA. Customer keeps: contracts, data model, integrations.**
Blockchain as a Service (BaaS).modernNote: The BaaS vendor landscape has consolidated hard since 2019 - most early managed-chain start-ups are gone, and the survivors are either cloud providers selling managed ledgers or specialist platforms that mostly sell software and services rather than raw BaaS. The enterprise market that expected rapid adoption instead stalled at pilot stage, so 'BaaS' today is a smaller, more infrastructure-flavoured business than the syllabus implies.

examAnswer.question: What is Blockchain as a Service? Explain what the BaaS provider actually runs, what the customer keeps, and why it is the default entry point for enterprises.
examAnswer.full:
Blockchain as a Service is a managed-service model: the provider runs the ledger - nodes, consensus, key custody, monitoring, upgrades and SLA - while the customer keeps its business logic and its data model. It is the difference between running your own generator and buying electricity from the grid: the network is someone else's maintenance problem.

**What the provider runs.**

**Nodes.** The provider creates the chain, selects the consensus and permissioning model, and provisions and sizes the node estate across cloud or on-premise infrastructure against the customer's availability target. It patches, upgrades, scales, fails over between regions and providers, and watches block times, peer counts and node health.

**Consensus and governance.** The provider operates the consensus client and the validator or ordering set, and owns the upgrade path - planned protocol versions and emergency patches.

**Key custody.** Generation, rotation, escrow, revocation and the signing policy, held in an HSM or cloud KMS. The provider, not the customer, is the trust boundary. This is the largest single transfer of risk in the arrangement.

**Monitoring and SLA.** Alerting, transaction failure rates, latency and cost, backed by a service-level agreement covering availability, throughput, support response time and incident severity, with credits for misses.

**What the customer keeps.** Its business logic in smart contracts, its own data model, its integration with ERP, core banking and identity systems, and the decision of what data to place on the ledger at all.

**The commercial exchange.** The customer buys a guaranteed service priced per transaction, per seat or per committed tier, instead of hiring blockchain operations staff and owning the infrastructure. Most enterprise chains are permissioned and tokenless, so there is no token revenue to rely on - the revenue is the managed-service fee.

**Why it is the default entry point.** Most firms want the capability, not the operational burden. BaaS converts a multi-year infrastructure and hiring programme into a contract with a SLA, and puts the uptime and security liability on the party best able to carry it.

**The honest trade-off.** The customer has bought certainty and paid for it with custody and control: the provider holds the keys and sets the upgrade schedule. That is the same trade as the electricity grid - and it is why a customer with regulatory reasons to own its keys, or with data-residency requirements, often ends up running the chain itself instead.

advantages: A designed token economy makes the demand for the token auditable: you can name the resource it buys and the fee that prices it.
Supply, distribution and vesting decide whether early insiders can dump, so they protect the price without needing to promise returns.
Value accrual - fee burn, fee sharing, staking rewards - ties the token to network usage instead of to narrative.
The regulatory classification is a checklist, not a matter of taste: it tells you which sale restrictions, disclosure duties and accounting rules apply before you design the raise.
Fee economics make the real burn rate and treasury runway a number the team can manage, rather than a hope.
limitations: A token can have perfect mechanics and still have no demand - the economics cannot manufacture users who want the service.
Burn-and-stake accrual models proved harder than advertised: on several major chains staking rewards exceeded burn, so the token was inflationary in practice while claiming to be deflationary.
Classification is legally expensive and fact-specific; the same token design can be classified differently in different jurisdictions.
High token valuations in the 2021 cycle came from monetary speculation, not from utility, which meant the market price was never a signal of the token economy working.
Emissions-funded networks survive only while the token price is high - the funding source and the price are correlated, so a price collapse removes the funding at the worst moment.
Token Economy.memoryTrick: **Classify, cap, distribute, give it a job, route the value, burn the fee, check the legal test** - seven moves, in that order.
Token Economy.modernNote: The regulatory line the syllabus draws has hardened since 2022: the SEC's 2023-24 settlements left essentially every publicly traded token as a security or an unregistered offering, and the EU's MiCA regime licenses token issuance and trading as a financial service with no broad utility exemption. So 'call it a utility token' is no longer a legal strategy - only genuinely network-functional tokens keep any non-financial treatment.

examAnswer.question: Explain the token economy: the classification of tokens, supply and distribution, value accrual, and where the regulatory line between a utility token and an investment token lies.
examAnswer.full:
A token economy is the design of a token's total supply, its distribution, the utility that creates demand for it, and the mechanism by which the value the network creates accrues to its holders, together with the regulatory classification that decides how it may be sold and traded. Four variables, and one legal test.

**1. Classify by the claim the token makes.** Utility - access to a network service. Security - a claim on an issuer such as equity, debt or a share of profit. Commodity-like - a store of value and means of exchange. The label is a description of the claim, not a marketing choice.

**2. Fix supply and the release schedule.** Hard cap or inflation; the genesis split; vesting and cliff for team and investors; reserves for ecosystem grants. A 5% annual inflation with no offsetting burn dilutes every holder who does not run a node.

**3. Distribute.** Genesis allocation across community, private sale, public sale and treasury; airdrops and early-user rewards. An airdrop with no utility to follow is a one-off sale that dumps on the market.

**4. Give the token a job.** Name the scarce resource it buys - bandwidth, storage, compute, transaction rights, node participation, governance weight. This is where demand for the service becomes demand for the token.

**5. Route the value to the holder.** Burn a fraction of transaction fees, distribute fees to stakers, pay staking rewards, or shrink supply. The network creating value is not the same as the token capturing it, and the second is what the holder actually owns. Worked example: a network taking a 0.1% fee on USD 10 transactions with 1,000 transactions a day burns USD 5 a day - real, but a rounding error next to a 5% inflation on a large supply.

**6. Set the fee economics.** Fee per unit of work, the fraction burned, the inflation offset by the burn, and the treasury runway in months at the current burn rate. This is the number the team manages.

**7. Place the regulatory line.** The test is whether buyers expect returns from the efforts of others. If they do, the token behaves like a security and is treated like one - Howey in the US, SEBI's collective-investment-scheme test in India - whatever the whitepaper calls it.

**Modern correction.** After the 2023-24 SEC settlements and MiCA in the EU, almost every publicly traded token is treated as a financial instrument, so the 'utility' label no longer buys an exemption. Only genuinely network-functional tokens keep non-financial treatment - which makes designing a real utility, rather than renaming a security, the only durable route.

advantages: It replaces a bet on the token price with a recurring operating cost, so the revenue is tied to usage and survives a price cycle.
The demand for the service creates the demand for the token automatically, without a marketing budget or an exchange listing campaign.
It is the only token model that survives a regulatory test as genuinely non-financial, because the token is consumed, not resold for profit.
A priced, scarce utility gives the network a real cost base, so node operators can be paid from fees rather than from emissions.
It makes the network's usage measurable: the fee bill is the KPI, and growth in fees is growth in demand.
limitations: The loop needs real scarcity. Most 'utilities' are copyable and unlimited - a name, a badge, a discount - so the token has no job.
Fees denominated in a volatile token cut the fiat value of the network's revenue exactly when the token price falls, so the model is procyclical in the worst way.
Users route around payment where they can - free tiers, off-chain settlement, forks - and every bypass weakens the loop.
The model penalises early adoption: users must pay in a token whose price is uncertain, so the first users subsidise the risk for everyone else.
The utility must be genuinely valuable to the user, which most chain-native utility is not - most real users pay fiat for something they actually want.
Utility Token Business Model.memoryTrick: **Service needs the token, token needs scarcity, token must pay the real cost - else the loop is open.**
Utility Token Business Model.modernNote: The utility-token thesis has been substantially tested since 2019 and mostly disappointed for consumer chains: real-world usage stayed far below what the token models assumed, and the surviving examples are narrow - storage and bandwidth markets (Filecoin, Arweave) and a small number of app-specific chains - where the token genuinely buys a metered resource. This is the most honest way to state the topic's evidence.

examAnswer.question: Explain the utility token business model. Describe the demand loop and the conditions under which the model breaks down.
examAnswer.full:
A utility token business model creates demand for a token by making the token the required payment or key for using a scarce network service, so demand for the service automatically becomes demand for the token. It is the gym-membership model: the fee only makes sense because the gym is useful and your slot is limited.

**The loop, in order.**

1. **Name the scarce resource.** Bandwidth, storage, compute, priority transaction space, node participation rights, or a hard cap on transactions per period.

2. **Make the token mandatory to use the service.** Fees are paid in the token, or tokens must be staked to qualify. Service usage is now token demand by construction.

3. **Tie the price to real work.** The fee scales with the work the network performs - per GB stored, per second of compute, per transaction - so the token behaves like an operating cost, not like a lottery ticket.

4. **The loop closes.** Users pay fees in the token; the token is spent to the network and burned or distributed to validators; the network grows and the service improves; more users arrive; each new user needs the service and so pulls more token demand.

**The conditions it needs.** The utility must be genuinely scarce, because unlimited free utility means the token has no job and no value. The token must pay a real cost - high enough to cover the node's operating cost - so that holding it is an operating expense rather than a pure bet on the price going up. And there must be real users who want the service; the loop is a consequence of demand, not a substitute for it.

**How it breaks down.** Thin utility leads users to route around the token - free tiers, off-chain settlement, forks - and each bypass weakens the loop. If the fee is set below the node's real cost, the network runs on emissions, which is a subsidy dressed as a model. And because fees are denominated in a volatile asset, a price collapse cuts the fiat value of the network's revenue at the moment the network is weakest.

**Worked example.** A storage network charging 1 token per GB-month, with a 100,000-token cap and 60% of fees burned, has a real utility, a real cost and a real accrual path. A social network whose only utility is registering a name on an unlimited ledger has none of the three - and the tokens it sells are simply an investment with a name attached.

advantages: High gross margin, because there is no per-customer hosting cost and no 24x7 operations team.
Near-zero operational load - no uptime obligation, no key custody risk, no incident response for someone else's chain.
Works for tokenless permissioned deployments, which is where most enterprise buyers actually are.
Scales with copies sold rather than with headcount, so growth is not linear in hiring.
The vendor is free to compete on product quality and integration depth rather than on who can operate a node estate.
limitations: No lock-in - the customer can move to an open-source equivalent, and price pressure from free tools is permanent.
The vendor captures none of the value created on the chain it enabled, so it is always last in the value chain.
The customer must still hire or contract for blockchain operations, so the total cost of ownership does not drop as much as the licence price suggests.
Shipping is a permanent cost: every customer is a claim on the roadmap, and security patches to old versions are unfunded work.
No network effect - the vendor does not get stronger as more customers adopt, unlike a token or platform model.
Blockchain-Based Software Products.memoryTrick: **Sell the brush, not the painting** - customer runs the chain, you collect the licence.
Blockchain-Based Software Products.modernNote: Most vendors that described themselves as blockchain software products in 2019 are now selling developer tooling, indexers, wallet and custody infrastructure, or have become consultancies - the standalone 'blockchain software product' category has largely been absorbed into general web3 and AI tooling.

examAnswer.question: Explain the blockchain-based software product business model and how it differs from BaaS.
examAnswer.full:
A blockchain-based software product business model sells code - a licence or a subscription - while the customer runs the nodes, hosts the smart contracts and pays the gas. It is selling a paintbrush rather than a painting service: you make the product once and sell many, and the customer does the messy work.

**How it works.** The vendor builds the product once - client libraries, indexers, explorers, contract templates, testing and deployment tooling, the smart-contract suite and the documentation - and licenses it, either as a perpetual licence with annual support or as a subscription covering updates, patches and support. The customer hosts it in its own environment, operates the nodes, holds its own keys, and pays the gas for every transaction it submits. The vendor keeps the economics: high gross margin with no per-customer hosting cost, no operations team and no SLA obligation, and its only permanent cost is shipping.

**The advantages.** High margin and near-zero operational load, no uptime liability, no key custody risk, no network effect needed, and it works for the tokenless permissioned deployments that most enterprise buyers actually run.

**The limitations.** Open-source equivalents cap the price, so the vendor must keep shipping and differentiate on support and integration depth. There is no lock-in and no share of the value the customer creates on the chain, so the vendor is always last in the value chain. And the customer still needs blockchain operations capability, so the total cost of ownership falls by less than the licence price suggests.

**How it differs from BaaS.** In exactly one place - who runs the chain. In BaaS the provider runs the nodes, consensus, keys, monitoring and the SLA; in a software product the customer runs the nodes, hosts the contracts and pays the gas, and the vendor's obligation ends at the release. Everything else follows from that: BaaS is a recurring managed-service fee with operational liability attached, whereas the software product is a one-off or annual payment with none.

advantages: No platform take-rate means lower trading costs for participants, which is a real competitive advantage when the network's whole proposition is cheap settlement.
The coordinator's revenue is decoupled from its own transactions, so it cannot be accused of profiting from the trades it coordinates.
Growth in the network raises the coordinator's income without requiring it to raise prices on its users.
There is no central platform holding user funds in the ordinary case, which removes a large single point of failure.
Direct participant-to-participant dealing removes the need for the platform's matching function entirely.
limitations: No transaction revenue means no guaranteed cash flow - the coordinator's income is only as stable as the token it depends on.
If the token never gains value, the coordinator's only revenue line disappears while the infrastructure costs remain.
With no platform take-rate to fund operations, the shared infrastructure falls back on token emissions or unpaid node operators - the free-rider problem returns in force.
Removing the trusted intermediary removes the dispute-resolution and recourse function too, and the protocol does not automatically replace it.
The model concentrates the coordinator's incentives on network size rather than network quality, which can push growth at the expense of safety.
P2P Blockchain Business Model.memoryTrick: **Paid by the ecosystem, not by the trade** - no take-rate means no guaranteed cash flow.
P2P Blockchain Business Model.modernNote: In practice the P2P class has split: some networks became regulated venues with a take-rate (exchange models) and some became pure infrastructure providers paid for by the ecosystem. Very few sustain a coordinator's income on token value alone without a regulated or institutional revenue line alongside it.

examAnswer.question: Explain the P2P blockchain business model and how the coordinator earns from the network rather than from the transactions.
examAnswer.full:
In a peer-to-peer blockchain business model, participants transact directly with each other over a shared ledger and the coordinator earns from the network itself rather than from a cut of the transactions. It is a marketplace where the organiser is paid by the market's growth rather than by a slice of each stallholder's sales.

**How it works.**

1. **Participants trade directly.** Buyer and seller transact with one another over the shared ledger. The ledger supplies the shared record of what was agreed and what was delivered - the function the trusted intermediary used to perform.

2. **No transaction fee is taken.** There is no platform transaction to tax: no take-rate, no spread, no per-trade fee. This is the structural difference from the marketplace model, not a discount on it.

3. **The coordinator earns from the network.** By holding or issuing the network token and benefiting from its value, or by charging for the infrastructure services the network needs - routing, liquidity provision, oracle feeds, node and staking services.

4. **The alignment.** Because its revenue grows with the health and size of the whole network rather than with its own transactions, the coordinator has an interest in keeping the rules fair and the participants solvent. It is paid by the ecosystem, not by the trade.

**The trade-off the model accepts.** With no transaction revenue there is no guaranteed cash flow, so the coordinator's income is as volatile as the token, and it must keep issuing or holding value to stay solvent. This is the price of removing the take-rate.

**The risk the model carries.** If the token never gains value, the coordinator's only revenue disappears - and with it the funding for the shared infrastructure. Participants then free-ride, because the shared record still has value to them while the cost of running it has no one attached to it. A P2P model without a working token-incentive layer is a public good with no funding mechanism.

**In the exam.** Name the revenue source first - token-related income or infrastructure fees paid by participants - and only then classify the model as P2P. And keep the contrast sharp: a marketplace takes a cut of the trades it brokers; the P2P coordinator takes no cut and is paid by the ecosystem.

advantages: The fastest route to revenue in this field - a signed engagement precedes a shipped product by months.
The firm learns the client's business, its compliance constraints and its data, which becomes the ground truth for any product it later builds.
Recurring managed-operations retainers turn a one-off project into an annuity and create the switching cost that keeps the client.
Advisory work is defensible because judgement and architecture knowledge cannot be cloned the way software can.
It works even where the market is not ready for products, since the buyer needs decisions and capability rather than a feature set.
limitations: Income is capped by headcount - the services trap - so growth means hiring, and margin does not scale like a software licence.
Selling hours creates no lock-in: the client can leave at the end of the engagement and take the knowledge with it.
The firm carries delivery risk, and blockchain projects have a poor record of being finished, so reputation can be damaged by engagements that do not land.
Clients can capture the learning and build the capability in-house, especially large banks that hire the consultants who advised them.
It consumes the founders' attention, which is exactly the attention needed to build the product that would escape the trap.

Blockchain Professional Services.modernNote: The consulting market for blockchain has shrunk with the end of the 2019-21 pilot wave - many of the firms that were built to sell advisory now sell AI, data and cloud implementation work, and blockchain is a line item inside a bigger engagement rather than a practice of its own.

examAnswer.question: Explain the three service lines in the blockchain professional services model, and the pitfall of selling hours instead of an outcome.
examAnswer.full:
Blockchain professional services is a revenue model that sells advisory, integration and managed operations for a project fee or a retainer, rather than selling infrastructure or software. It is the plumbing company: you can charge by the hour of wrenching, or by the working kitchen you leave behind, and only one of those keeps you booked.

**The three service lines.**

**1. Advisory.** Architecture and governance: whether a chain is needed at all, which business model fits (BaaS, software or P2P), permissioning and identity design, token design where relevant, and the governance rules that decide who can change what and who can exit.

**2. Integration.** Wiring the chain into the client's existing estate: ERP, core banking and identity and KYC systems, data feeds, wallet and key infrastructure, and the smart contracts that encode the business rules. This is the largest and most repeatable line, because integration work recurs at every client.

**3. Managed operations.** Running and upgrading the network for the client under a retainer: node operations, monitoring, key rotation, incident response, protocol upgrades, and the SLA.

**The pricing and the trap.** The revenue is project-based or retainer-based - the firm is paid for effort and expertise rather than for network usage. The classic trap is selling hours: that caps income at the number of billable people and creates no lock-in, because the client has no reason to stay once the project ends. Selling a defined outcome - a working settlement, a compliant integration, a network running under an SLA - or a recurring managed-service retainer breaks that ceiling, because the client is buying a result and a continued relationship.

**Worked example.** A bank paying a consultancy 40% of a USD 1m integration project is project revenue. The same firm retained at USD 20,000 a month to run the chain and renew the SLA is managed-operations revenue - and the second is the business that scales.

**The honest limit.** Services margin does not scale like a software licence: growth is hiring-driven, and the firm must convert engagements into products, platforms or retainers or it stays a consultancy with a limited ceiling. That is why most firms in this space run a services arm deliberately - it funds and de-risks the product, it should not be the destination.

advantages: Atomic delivery versus payment removes the principal-versus-payment problem entirely - there is no window in which one leg has settled and the other has not.
It cuts the correspondent chain, so the per-hop fees and the per-hop days come out of the payment.
With both legs settling together, the pre-funded nostro liquidity the correspondent chain demands can be cut - a direct balance-sheet saving.
A shared ledger gives a single agreed, real-time record of accounts and ownership, which also compresses reconciliation and reporting.
Settlement finality is a property of the protocol rather than of a particular institution's policy, which is the same property for every participant.
limitations: The back-office work does not disappear, it moves: reconciliation becomes on-chain state verification, and the bank still pays for on-chain KYC/AML, key management, node operations and node cost.
Compliance gets harder in one respect - addresses are pseudonymous, so attribution and AML monitoring need new tooling and new controls.
Liquidity and collateral still have to be provisioned, so the working-capital saving is real but smaller than the marketing usually implies.
The model works for high-value, multi-party, cross-border flows; for small-value retail payments the saved fee is smaller than the cost of running a node.
Governance of a shared ledger adds a new governance problem - who can change the rules of a ledger that holds the assets of many banks - and forks are not an option for settled balances.
Interoperability with the existing core banking and payments estate is the real integration cost, and it is paid before any saving is realised.

This is exactly the distinction the syllabus draws between the cost of moving funds and the removal of the bank.

examAnswer.question: Explain how a blockchain can be applied to banking and financial transactions. Cover settlement, the principal-versus-payment problem, atomic delivery versus payment, KYC/AML, the real cost model for a bank's back office, and PvP risk.
examAnswer.full:
A shared ledger applied to finance changes the settlement leg of a payment. It is the difference between writing a cheque and both parties swapping money at the same instant: the cheque can bounce, the simultaneous swap cannot.

**1. The old path and what settlement costs.** A payment hops through correspondent banks. Each hop takes a fee, takes a day or two, and adds its own credit risk - if one bank in the chain fails, the payment fails. Because the two legs settle days apart, each bank must pre-fund its position across the chain in nostro balances, which ties up balance sheet and creates principal-versus-payment risk: the seller may have delivered and the buyer may have paid, but the two legs are days apart, so somebody is exposed in the gap.

**2. PvP risk defined.** Principal-versus-payment risk is the risk that the buyer pays and the seller never delivers, or delivers and never gets paid, because the two legs of the trade settle at different times. This is what makes real-time gross settlement expensive: RTGS settles each payment individually and immediately, so liquidity must be pre-funded for every payment.

**3. Atomic delivery versus payment.** On a shared ledger the asset transfer and the payment instruction change state in the SAME transaction. Both succeed or both fail together. There is no window between the legs, so PvP risk is removed rather than reduced.

**4. The consequence for liquidity.** Because both legs settle together, the pre-funded liquidity that correspondent banking demands can be cut or eliminated. This is the direct balance-sheet saving and the strongest argument for the model.

**5. The trust substitution.** One agreed record of accounts and ownership, held by consensus, replaces the chain of implied trust in each correspondent. The network's consensus does the work the correspondent chain did - but only for the participants in that network.

**6. KYC/AML does not go away - it moves onto the chain.** Compliance becomes screening against a traceable, pseudonymised identity layer rather than against the bank's own customer database. This is a new technical cost, and in one respect it is harder: attribution is harder than in a conventional database, so monitoring tooling and controls have to be rebuilt.

**7. The real cost model for the back office.** Reconciliation becomes on-chain state verification; key management, node operations and node cost are new line items; liquidity or collateral still has to be provisioned. The work is not eliminated, it is relocated and partly automated. The business case is therefore about the cost of moving funds and the capital tied up in settlement - not about removing the bank.

**8. Where it fits.** Strong for high-value, multi-party, cross-border settlement with a long correspondent chain and an expensive PvP window. Weak for small-value retail payments, where the saved fee is smaller than the cost of running a node - which is why the real deployments have been in tokenised deposits, repo and interbank settlement rather than in consumer payments.
